title: Note-taking that works
examples: How do I know if my notes are good enough for a test?
What is the difference between summarizing and just rewriting?
Can I use this method for history or science?

explain.say: Today we are learning how to take notes that actually help you remember things.

items: Notes Area: Main ideas and details
Cue/Question Column: Key words and prompts
Summary Area: Overall meaning in your own words

explain.say: The Cornell method divides your page into three useful sections for learning.

items: Example: Photosynthesis | Light energy needed | Process converts light to food

explain.say: After taking notes, you must summarise the main points at the bottom of the page.
When you review, write potential questions in the narrow cue column on the left.
For example, if reading about gravity, you might write 'What causes gravity?' in the cue column.
In real life, you use this when listening to a long lecture or watching a documentary.

faq.q: How long should the summary section be?
faq.a: The summary should be a few sentences long. It captures the whole page's meaning simply.
asks: Do I write a paragraph at the bottom?
How much should the summary take up?

faq.q: Should I write down every single word I hear?
faq.a: No, you should only write down the main ideas. Use your own words to explain the concepts.
asks: Is it okay to use abbreviations?

faq.q: What if I don't know what question to write in the cue column?
faq.a: You can write a keyword that reminds you of the idea. This prompts your memory when you study later.
asks: What if the topic is very broad?
Can I write a date instead?

faq.q: Does this method work for reading books or just lectures?
faq.a: It works for both. You read a section, then use the method to organize the key points you found.
asks: Can I use it for textbooks?
Is it only for oral presentations?

faq.q: When should I fill in the cue column?
faq.a: It is best to fill this in after the lesson. This forces you to process and question what you just learned.
asks: Do I wait until I study to fill it?
Is it better to do it right away?

facts: Cornell notes divide notes into three sections: notes, cues, and summary.
Summarising means restating the main idea in your own words.
Writing questions in the margin helps you actively recall information.
This method encourages you to review and test yourself regularly.

quiz.say: When using Cornell notes, what should the summary area contain?

options.show: A brief overview of the entire page's content.
options.say: A brief overview of the entire page's content.

options.show: A list of all the facts mentioned.
options.say: A list of all the facts mentioned.

options.show: Only the most important vocabulary words.
options.say: Only the most important vocabulary words.

options.show: A full rewrite of the original text.
options.say: A full rewrite of the original text.

quiz.why: The summary forces you to synthesize everything into one short takeaway.

wrong.1: This is too much detail and defeats the purpose of summarising.
wrong.2: Vocabulary belongs in the notes area, not the summary.
wrong.3: Rewriting is not summarising; it is just copying the structure.

quiz.say: If you are taking notes on the water cycle, what should you place in the cue column?
quiz.why: Writing a question prompts your brain to remember the answer later.

wrong.0: The definition belongs in the main notes area, not the question column.
wrong.1: Diagrams are visual aids, but the cue column needs text prompts.
wrong.2: This is just a keyword; a question is more effective for recall.

quiz.say: A student writes 'The Earth orbits the Sun' in the notes area, and writes 'What path does Earth take?' in the cue column. What is the best action for the summary?

options.show: A sentence stating Earth follows a path around the Sun.
options.say: A sentence stating Earth follows a path around the Sun.

options.show: Writing 'The Earth orbits the Sun' again.
options.say: Writing 'The Earth orbits the Sun' again.

quiz.why: The summary must combine the key concepts from both the notes and the cue.

wrong.0: This is just a list of nouns, not a summary of the action.
wrong.2: This is repetitive and does not show understanding.
wrong.3: The summary is a crucial step for checking overall understanding.
